statement.p: Show that T(u,v)=(u^2-v^2,2uv) maps the triangle =\lbrace (u,v): 0\le v\le u\le 1\rbrace to the domain \mathcal{D} bounded by x=0, y=0,
and y^2=4-4x. Use T to evaluate \int\!\!\int _{\mathcal{D}}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\, dx\,dy Answer :

static.solution:
{\mathcal{D}}_0 is mapped to the boundary of \mathcal{D}.
With u_0=1,\quad x_0=1,\quad and y_0=2
We have x={u}^2-{v}^2\quad\text{and}\quad y=2uv The line v=u is mapped to the following set: (x,y)=({u}^2-{u}^2,2{u}^2)=(0,2{u}^2)\quad \Rightarrow\quad x=0,\quad y\ge 0
That is, the image of the line u=v is the positive y-axis. The line v=0 is mapped to the following set: ( x,y )=({u}^2,0)\quad\Rightarrow\quad x={u}^2,\quad y=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad y=0,\quad x\ge 0 Thus, the line v=0 is mapped to the positive x-axis. We now show that the vertical line u=1 is mapped to the curve {y}^2+4x=4.
The image of the line u=1 is the following set: (x,y)=(1-{v}^2,2v)\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=1-{v}^2,\quad y=2v We substitute v=\frac{y}{2} in the equation x=1-{v}^2 to obtain x=1-{\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)}^2=1-\frac{{y}^2}{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 4x=4-{y}^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad {y}^2+4x=4 Since the boundary of {\mathcal{D}}_0 is mapped to the boundary of \mathcal{D}, we conclude that the domain {\mathcal{D}}_0 is mapped by T to the domain \mathcal{D} in the xy-plane.
We now compute the integral \int\!\!\int _{\mathcal{D}} \sqrt{{x}^2+{y}^2} \,dx \,dy.
We express the function f( x,y )=\sqrt{{x}^2+{y}^2} in terms of the new variables u and v: \begin{array}{rcl} f( x,y ) = \sqrt{{({u}^2-{v}^2)}^2+{( 2uv )}^2}\amp =\amp \sqrt{{u}^4-2{u}^2{v}^2+{v}^4+4{u}^2{v}^2}\\ \amp =\amp \sqrt{{u}^4+2{u}^2{v}^2+{v}^4}= \sqrt{{({u}^2+{v}^2)}^2}\\ \amp =\amp {u}^2+{v}^2 \end{array} We compute the Jacobian of T: \mathrm{Jac}(T) = \frac{\partial ( x,y )}{\partial ( u,v )}= \left|\begin{array}{rr} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\ \noalign{\medskip} \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{cc} 2u\amp -2v\\ 2v\amp 2u\end{array}\right|=4{u}^2+4{v}^2= 4({u}^2+{v}^2)
With u_0=1
\begin{array}{rcl} \int\!\!\int _{\mathcal{D}} \sqrt{{x}^2+{y}^2} \,dx \,dy \amp =\amp \int\!\!\int _{\mathcal{D}_0} ({u}^2+{v}^2)\cdot 4({u}^2+{v}^2) \,du \,dv\\ \amp =\amp 4\int_0^{1} \int_0^{u} ({u}^4+2{u}^2{v}^2+{v}^4) \,dv \,du\\ \amp =\amp 4\int_0^{1} {u}^4v+\frac{2}{3}{u}^2{v}^3+\frac{{v}^5}{5}\bigg|_{v=0}^{u} \,du\\ \amp =\amp 4\int_0^{1} \left({u}^5+\frac{2}{3}{u}^5+\frac{{u}^5}{5}\right) \,du\\ \amp =\amp 4\int_0^{1} \frac{28}{15}{u}^5 \,du\\ \amp =\amp \frac{112}{15}\cdot \frac{{u}^6}{6}\bigg|_0^{1}\\ \amp =\amp \frac{56}{45} \approx 1.24444 \end{array}
